title: Understanding sin. Cultivating a life of love.
intro: What does the Bible call sin? How can we recognize attitudes that harm our relationship with God and our neighbour? Here, study connects with examples and paths of repentance, care and making amends.
summaryNote: These explanations are the platform’s summaries and applications, not literal quotations. Open the references to read passages in context. This is not a complete list of every sin.
definition: From a biblical perspective, sin involves transgressing God’s will and practising injustice. It can also involve omitting the good we know we ought to do. Examination includes actions, words, cultivated desires and omissions rather than religious appearances alone.
idolatry: Biblical faith rejects giving another what belongs to God. The problem also appears when money, power or interests become absolute and are used to justify harming someone. Colossians associates greed with idolatry; Jesus contrasts serving God and money.
idolatryExample: For example, defending your faith does not authorize threats, humiliation or attacks against people who believe differently. You can disagree firmly and still treat others with dignity. Hatred and violence must be examined as actions without condemning an entire group.
images: Christian traditions interpret the use of images differently. The Catholic Catechism distinguishes veneration of images from the worship owed to God alone (2132). When comparing practices, identify the tradition and its teaching rather than assuming each person’s intention.
imagesAction: Read the Catholic explanation of images
gravityTitle: Mortal, venial and capital sins: what is the difference?
gravity: In Catholic teaching, mortal sin requires all three: grave matter, full knowledge and deliberate consent. Venial sin involves less serious matter or a lack of full knowledge/consent in grave matter. A list of acts alone cannot judge someone’s responsibility.
gravityNote: Other Christian communities do not necessarily use this classification in the same way. It is presented here as Catholic teaching, with its source.
graveTitle: Examples of serious conduct to study
graveIntro: The references help recognize wrongdoing and seek change. The seriousness of conduct and personal responsibility must not be confused with an automatic judgement of someone’s spiritual situation.
examples: Attacking life, threatening and humiliating harm our neighbour. Jesus also challenges anger expressed through insults.
Stop aggression and seek safety and help. Reconciliation does not require remaining in a violent situation.
Taking what belongs to others, deceiving for gain and bearing false witness destroy trust and cause harm.
Acknowledge the wrongdoing, correct the information and seek to make amends responsibly.
Adultery, exploitation and relationships that disregard others’ dignity contradict faithfulness and care.
Set boundaries, leave harmful conduct behind and seek responsible guidance.
Placing profit above justice can lead to exploitation, withholding what is owed and treating people as means to wealth.
Practise fair agreements and honesty. Share according to your abilities and responsibilities.
Slander, contempt and words used to destroy do not fit love of neighbour.
Pause, avoid sending an insult and try to express the disagreement truthfully and respectfully.
Omission in the face of need
Knowing we can do good and deliberately ignoring it also calls for examination. Care must consider what is actually within our reach.
Choose one possible act of help without exposing or pressuring the person receiving it.
causesTitle: What can lead us into wrongdoing?
causesIntro: James describes a progression from cultivated desire to sin. In practice, it is worth noticing choices, habits and excuses. Environments influence opportunities, but a quiet place does not guarantee freedom from anger and religious appearances do not guarantee integrity.
causes: Wanting an advantage and justifying the harm it causes.
Repeating conduct until we stop considering its consequences.
Giving in to group pressure or the need to appear superior.
Holding resentment and choosing to nourish revenge.
Ignoring correction and seeking only people who confirm our choices.
Confusing a temptation or involuntary thought with a deliberate decision: feeling or thinking something is not automatically choosing to act on it.
capitalTitle: The seven capital sins in everyday life
capitalNote: Capital sins are vices that foster other sins; they do not automatically equal mortal sins.
capitalIntro: We connect the teaching with concrete actions: recognize harm, cultivate a virtue and prepare conditions for acting better. These examples are applications, not diagnoses of people.
capital: Pride
Humility
Seeking superiority and despising others can prevent listening and accepting correction.
Listen carefully to an opinion, acknowledge a mistake and thank someone for help.
Avarice and greed
Generosity and justice
Placing accumulation above everything can crowd out sharing and honesty.
Pay what is owed, refuse unfair advantages and set aside help within your means.
Envy
Gratitude and goodwill
Nurtured comparison can turn into resentment and a desire to diminish others’ good.
Recognize someone’s qualities without turning the conversation into competition.
Destructive anger
Gentleness and self-control
Anger can become insult, threat or aggression when we choose to feed it and hurt others.
Reduce confrontational stimuli, pause and return to the conversation safely and respectfully.
Lust
Respect and faithfulness
Reducing someone to an object and betraying commitments harms relationships and dignity.
Set limits around harmful conduct and choose respectful relationships without exploitation.
Gluttony
Temperance and care
Studying temperance invites examination of excess, waste and failure to share. Someone’s body does not reveal their moral life.
Care for your diet according to your needs and access, avoid waste and share when possible.
Sloth or spiritual neglect
Achievable diligence
Deliberately abandoning responsibility must be distinguished from needing rest or facing real limitations.
Choose an achievable task and ask for support. Fatigue, ADHD, depression and illness do not automatically mean moral neglect.
fastingTitle: Fasting, gluttony and food: how can we connect them with care?
fasting: In Matthew 6:16–18, Jesus teaches fasting without religious display. Isaiah 58 connects fasting with justice, liberation from oppression and sharing bread. The platform invites reflection on humility, self-control and generosity through these passages.
fastingHealth: Religious fasting does not guarantee weight loss, diabetes prevention or freedom from illness. Weight and diagnoses do not measure holiness or show that someone practises gluttony. People with diabetes should consult their health team before fasting; do not change food intake or medication on your own to meet a website challenge.
fastingPractice: One possible step: examine waste, care for a meal within your circumstances and share something within your means. If you wish to fast, discuss the practice with your community and respect health guidance. No duration, competition or weight target is proposed here.
changeIntro: The purpose is to seek truth, forgiveness and change rather than remain trapped in accusation. Zacchaeus’ story connects meeting Jesus with making amends; James calls us to put the Word into practice.
changeSteps: Recognize a concrete attitude without reducing your entire identity to it.
Turn to God in prayer and seek guidance in your faith community.
Stop the harm and respect the safety of those affected.
Make amends responsibly where possible; asking forgiveness does not oblige another person to resume a relationship.
Prepare a habit and environment that support change. Seek qualified help if needed.
careNote: This study must not be used to humiliate, diagnose or persecute people. If the subject causes intense distress, you can take a break and seek human support.

sourceText: An introductory Christian summary. Mortal/venial classification and Catholic teaching on images identify their tradition. Specific pastoral questions call for accompaniment without automatic verdicts about people.

everydayTitle: From church to life: recognizing wrongdoing in daily situations
everydayIntro: Knowing a name is not enough: study gains meaning when we notice the attitude, the harm and a possible way forward. These situations are illustrative, not real accounts or a tool for judging other people’s consciences.
reasonText: Religious practice can teach us, but attending worship alone does not guarantee consistency outside it. We can ask: what am I seeking? Which means am I using? Who is affected? Am I respecting truth and dignity? What just and loving action can I choose now? There is no need to monitor every thought without rest; the purpose is to recognize concrete choices and learn to act.
everyday: When looking turns into coveting
You notice an attractive person or something you would like to own. Noticing is not the same as deciding to exploit someone, betray a commitment or take what belongs to another.
Examine what you choose to nurture: objectifying someone, justifying betrayal or developing deception to obtain what you want. Temptation does not make theft or violence inevitable.
Acknowledge desire without treating it as an order. Respect people and commitments; stop conduct that causes harm. If the pursuit has become a harmful habit, ask for support to change.
Matthew 5:27–30 · James 1:13–15
Food, waste and sharing
Food is available, and someone is in need. The examination is not about measuring the eater’s body but asking how resources are used and whether we can share responsibly.
Waste for show or deliberately refusing possible help can reveal indifference. Food needs vary; eating what is needed or treating illness is not a moral failure.
Arrange a meal within your circumstances, care for what can be used and offer possible help without policing someone’s plate or humiliating their body.
Isaiah 58:7 · 1 John 3:17–18
Anger in conversation or online
A disagreement brings anger. You can acknowledge the feeling without sending a threat, exposing someone or turning conflict into aggression.
Notice when the intention shifts from clarifying a problem to causing hurt. A less provocative environment may help, but choosing boundaries and ways to respond also matters.
Pause before posting, check what you understood and revisit the issue respectfully when it is safe. If harm was caused, acknowledge it and seek to make amends.
Ephesians 4:26–32 · Proverbs 15:1
Earning more and forgetting those nearby
Wanting a better life or saving for real needs does not automatically equal greed. The problem appears when profit matters more than justice and dignity.
Examine fraud, withholding what is owed, exploitation and the idea that any means is acceptable for accumulation. Generosity does not replace honesty in earning.
Honour fair agreements, recognize rights and choose how to help within your means. Do not use a donation to conceal harm caused to someone.
Political arguments while a neighbour needs help
Debating politics and seeking social change can be part of responsibility for the common good. Disagreeing is not in itself a sin.
Examination begins when lies, humiliation, dehumanization, threats or corruption enter the defence of a position. Also ask whether the dispute excuses ignoring a need we can meet.
Check information before sharing it, criticize proposals without denying people’s dignity and choose a concrete act of care. Public discussion and solidarity can go together.
Ephesians 4:25–32 · James 2:14–17
Doing good to appear superior
A generous action can be good; recognition does not automatically make it false. But motives deserve examination when public image matters more than the person being helped.
Exposing someone’s pain for approval, using religion to claim superiority and rejecting all correction can foster pride. A recipient’s dignity is not publicity material.
Ask permission where appropriate, protect privacy and serve when no one is watching too. Be willing to learn from those you want to help.
Matthew 6:1–4 · Philippians 2:3–8
Comparison, envy and discouragement
Seeing someone else’s achievement may bring discomfort or sadness. That feeling does not force you to despise them or prove your own life has lost value.
Notice whether you begin inventing faults, spreading comments or wishing harm to diminish the other person’s achievement.
Acknowledge the emotion, reduce harmful comparisons and value an achievable step on your own journey. You can celebrate another person’s good and ask for support yourself.
James 3:13–18 · Romans 12:15
Resting or abandoning what I can do?
You have a responsibility, but you may also be tired, ill or without the resources to fulfil it. These circumstances deserve honest consideration.
Deliberate neglect should not automatically be confused with depression, ADHD, exhaustion or health limitations. Examine what is actually achievable without demanding impossible performance.
Choose a small step, arrange help and respect necessary rest. When you can act, turn learning into practical care.
Romans 12:9–13 · Mark 6:30–32
